applied.problem: It says fuel energy leaves only three ways and the bold line says every kilowatt leaves as work, cooling or exhaust; real engines also shed heat from the hot casing, and the [^3] quote is about heat into work, not all the fuel.
A motor's losses are not all in the windings and core: friction and windage in the bearings and air are heat too, which Dan as an electrician will know; 'mostly' keeps it true.

The marine paper calls large two-strokes at their efficiency close to Carnot's limits, which does not fit a flame-to-surroundings limit; the view should not pin the flame choice on marine researchers.

notes.problem: Seawater's 3,850 J per kg per °C and water's 4,200 are marked constant with no lesson source; both are in the research (R21, R6) but the frozen sources list does not carry them, so the worked example's key figure is uncited.

3,850 J per kg per °C is the lecture's 'about' figure; common seawater tables give nearer 3,990 at 35 salinity, which would make the cooler flow about 7.5 kg/s. The 7.8 kg/s answer errs on more flow, so it is safe, but a later rebuild could cite a table value.
